---
title: "Variable selection and big data"
subtitle: "Lecture 11"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can decide, for a regression with far more candidate
predictors than theory can rule in or out, which ones the data actually support,
without enumerating every possible subset or pretending that keeping them all and
shrinking them is the same thing.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

Attach to each coefficient $\beta_j$ a latent inclusion indicator $\gamma_j \in \{0,1\}$
and a two-component Normal prior, a narrow spike when $\gamma_j = 0$ and a wide slab
when $\gamma_j = 1$. Conditional on the current draw of $\beta_j$, the indicator's full
conditional is
$$
\frac{\Pr(\gamma_j = 1 \mid \beta_j, \text{rest})}{\Pr(\gamma_j = 0 \mid \beta_j, \text{rest})}
= \underbrace{\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}}_{\text{prior odds}} \times
\underbrace{\frac{p(\beta_j \mid \gamma_j = 1)}{p(\beta_j \mid \gamma_j = 0)}}_{\text{Bayes factor}} .
$$
A Gibbs sampler that cycles this indicator alongside the coefficients and the error
variance explores the space of models by wandering rather than enumerating it. The
difficulty is that the answer this delivers, a probability of inclusion for every
candidate, depends on the prior odds and on which other candidates are competing for
the same explanatory role, so it is not read off like a p-value and does not mean the
same thing in isolation as it does within the full candidate set.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. state why exhaustive model comparison is infeasible once the number of candidate
   predictors is moderate, and quantify the multiple-testing cost of screening them one
   at a time;
2. derive the spike-and-slab hierarchy and the Normal full conditional of the
   coefficient vector given the inclusion indicators;
3. derive the inclusion indicator's full conditional as prior odds times a Bayes
   factor, and say what the Occam-penalty term in that factor is doing;
4. implement stochastic search variable selection as a three-block Gibbs sampler and
   compute posterior inclusion probabilities and a median-probability model from its
   output;
5. diagnose, from the joint distribution of two correlated candidates' indicators,
   when a low marginal inclusion probability reflects genuine absence and when it
   reflects competition between substitutes;
6. compare the sparse posterior against an unrestricted fit out of sample, and state
   what the comparison does and does not establish about whether the world is sparse.

Week 11 of 15, paired with the [Week 11 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/11-variable-selection.qmd). The chapter uses the
conjugate Normal-inverse-Gamma regression posterior of Lecture 2 as its computational
core and the shrinkage intuition of Lecture 6; no new sampler beyond an ordinary
three-block Gibbs sweep is required.

## Motivation: forty-eight candidates for one bank's returns {#sec-motivation}

A risk manager wants to know how much of a bank portfolio's monthly return is spanned
by the rest of the economy, and which industries carry that span. The Kenneth French
industry classification gives forty-nine portfolios; take the banking industry as the
target and the other forty-eight as candidate regressors. Lecture 9 built posteriors
that averaged over a manageable handful of specifications. Here there is no small list
of specifications to average over. Any subset of forty-eight candidates is an
admissible model, and the natural first move, fit the regression with everything in it
and look at which coefficients come out large, is worth seeing fail before a repair is
proposed.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
ind = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_industry49_monthly.parquet").loc["1970-01":]
rf_m = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")["rf"].reindex(ind.index)
exc = ind.sub(rf_m, axis=0)

TARGET, SPLIT = "banks", "2009-12"
y_raw, X_raw = exc[TARGET], exc.drop(columns=[TARGET])
ind_names = list(X_raw.columns)
y_tr_raw, X_tr_raw = y_raw.loc[:SPLIT].to_numpy(), X_raw.loc[:SPLIT].to_numpy()
mx, sx = X_tr_raw.mean(0), X_tr_raw.std(0)
my, sy = y_tr_raw.mean(), y_tr_raw.std()
Xi, yi = (X_tr_raw - mx) / sx, (y_tr_raw - my) / sy
n_i, p_i = Xi.shape
XtX_i, Xty_i = Xi.T @ Xi, Xi.T @ yi

b_ols_i = np.linalg.solve(XtX_i, Xty_i)
resid_ols = yi - Xi @ b_ols_i
C_ind = np.corrcoef(Xi.T)
iu = np.triu_indices(p_i, 1)
ev_i = np.linalg.eigvalsh(XtX_i / n_i)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
ax.bar(np.arange(p_i), b_ols_i, color="0.45")
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(p_i)); ax.set_xticklabels(ind_names, rotation=90, fontsize=5)
ax.set_ylabel("OLS coefficient"); ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.6)
ax.set_title("Least squares on all 48 candidate industries")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"target: {TARGET}; {p_i} candidate industries; {n_i} training months "
      f"{exc.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {SPLIT}")
print(f"OLS: {np.sum(np.abs(b_ols_i) > 0.1)} of {p_i} coefficients exceed 0.1 "
      f"standard deviations in absolute value, largest {np.abs(b_ols_i).max():.3f}")
print(f"pairwise correlations among the 48 candidates: mean {np.abs(C_ind[iu]).mean():.3f}, "
      f"max {np.abs(C_ind[iu]).max():.3f} "
      f"({ind_names[iu[0][np.argmax(np.abs(C_ind[iu]))]]} and "
      f"{ind_names[iu[1][np.argmax(np.abs(C_ind[iu]))]]})")
print(f"condition number of the standardised design: {ev_i.max()/ev_i.min():.0f}")
```

Least squares puts a nonzero-looking coefficient on nearly every one of the forty-eight
industries, with the largest reaching more than a third of a standard deviation, and
the bar chart shows no natural break between "clearly relevant" and "clearly
irrelevant" bars: the coefficients simply decay smoothly from the largest to the
smallest with no gap to cut at. That is not a sign of forty-eight real economic
channels into bank returns. The candidates are correlated with each other at $0.565$ on
average and up to $0.876$ at the extreme, the condition number of the design is in the
hundreds, and Lecture 6 already showed what a design like this does to least squares:
it spreads the fit across correlated columns more or less arbitrarily, assigning a
coefficient to whichever column happened to align best with the noise in this
particular sample. A coefficient of this kind is not evidence that an industry belongs
in the model, and there are $2^{48}$ subsets of these forty-eight candidates, so
checking every alternative fit by hand is not an option either.

## The problem: too many models, too many chances to find one that fits {#sec-problem}

### Result R-11.1: the model space and the multiplicity it creates

With $p$ candidate regressors, and any subset admissible as a model, the model space
has $2^p$ members: $p=20$ gives about a million, $p=48$ gives $2.8 \times 10^{14}$, and
a realistic factor zoo with $p \approx 300$ gives more models than there are atoms in
the observable universe. Enumeration is not merely slow, it is impossible at any
computational budget worth discussing. Separately, and independently of the search
problem, screening $p$ candidates one at a time at significance level $\alpha$ produces
an expected
$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{false rejections}] = \alpha\, p_0
$$
spurious findings whenever $p_0$ of the $p$ candidates are truly unrelated to the
outcome, so a screen of even a modest zoo manufactures a short list of "significant"
predictors out of pure noise, and reporting only the winners of that screen presents
numbers selected for their extremeness rather than their truth.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The first claim is counting: a subset of a $p$-element set is specified by an
independent binary choice, in or out, for each element, so the number of subsets is
$2 \times 2 \times \cdots \times 2 = 2^p$. No structure in the model, and no cleverness
in the search algorithm, reduces this count; what a stochastic search can do, and what
the rest of this chapter builds, is visit a representative sample of high-probability
models without needing to enumerate the rest, which is a different task from counting
them.

The second claim is a property of independent hypothesis tests under their null. If
candidate $j$ is truly irrelevant, a test at level $\alpha$ rejects its null with
probability exactly $\alpha$ by construction, regardless of what the other $p-1$
candidates are, so the indicator of a false rejection for candidate $j$ is a Bernoulli
random variable with mean $\alpha$. Summing over the $p_0$ truly irrelevant candidates
and using linearity of expectation, which requires no independence assumption between
the tests at all,
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{j: \text{truly null}} \mathbb{1}\{\text{reject } j\}\Big]
= \sum_{j: \text{truly null}} \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{1}\{\text{reject } j\}\big]
= \alpha\, p_0,
$$
which is the displayed result. At $\alpha = 0.05$ and $p_0 = 1000$ candidates all
genuinely unrelated to the outcome, the expected number of spurious five-percent
findings is fifty, and nothing about the derivation requires the candidates to be
independent of one another; correlation among them changes the variance of the count of
false rejections but not its mean. A procedure that reports the winners of such a screen
without correcting for how many were tried is reporting noise dressed as discovery, and
the correction has to come from somewhere: either a formal multiple-testing adjustment
or, as the rest of this chapter builds, a prior that prices in the search before any
data are seen.
:::

The two halves of R-11.1 compound rather than cancel. Even if a search procedure could
somehow visit every one of the $2^{48}$ models fitted to the industry data, comparing
them by which one achieves the best in-sample fit would be exactly the data-mining
exercise the second half of the result warns against, at a scale the first half says is
already uncomputable. What is needed is a single coherent object that prices the
multiplicity in advance and explores the resulting posterior without visiting every
model, which is what the next section builds.

## Methodology: a prior on whether each coefficient belongs, and how to search with it {#sec-methodology}

### Result R-11.2: the spike-and-slab hierarchy and its Normal full conditional

For the regression $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2
I_n)$, attach a latent inclusion indicator to every coefficient,
$$
\beta_j \mid \gamma_j \sim (1-\gamma_j)\,\mathcal{N}(0, \tau_j^2)
+ \gamma_j\,\mathcal{N}(0, c^2\tau_j^2),
\qquad \gamma_j \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi),
\qquad \sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0),
$$
with $\tau_j^2$ small, the spike, and $c^2\tau_j^2$ large, the slab, $c \gg 1$.
Collecting the implied prior variances into $D_\gamma = \operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,
d_p)$, $d_j = (1-\gamma_j)\tau_j^2 + \gamma_j c^2 \tau_j^2$, gives $\beta \mid \gamma \sim
\mathcal{N}(0, D_\gamma)$, and conditional on $\gamma$ and $\sigma^2$ the coefficient
vector has the ordinary conjugate Normal posterior of Lecture 2 with this diagonal prior
covariance in place of a general one,
$$
\beta \mid \gamma, \sigma^2, y \sim \mathcal{N}(b_1, B_1), \qquad
B_1 = \Big(D_\gamma^{-1} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}X^\top X\Big)^{-1}, \qquad
b_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}B_1 X^\top y.
$$
Every coefficient stays in the design matrix regardless of $\gamma_j$; an "excluded"
coefficient is one drawn from a prior so tight that it is forced near zero, not one
removed from the regression.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Conditional on $\gamma$, the prior $\beta \mid \gamma \sim \mathcal{N}(0, D_\gamma)$ is
an ordinary Normal prior with a diagonal, possibly heterogeneous, covariance matrix.
The log posterior kernel is
$$
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y - X\beta)^\top(y-X\beta) - \frac12 \beta^\top D_\gamma^{-1}\beta
+ \text{const},
$$
and collecting the quadratic and linear terms in $\beta$ exactly as in the derivation of
the conjugate regression posterior of Lecture 2, with $B_0^{-1}$ there replaced by
$D_\gamma^{-1}$ here and the prior mean $b_0$ set to zero, gives $B_1^{-1} =
D_\gamma^{-1} + X^\top X/\sigma^2$ and $b_1 = B_1 X^\top y/\sigma^2$, the displayed
result. The only change from the single-prior case already derived in Lecture 2 is that
the prior precision is a diagonal matrix that differs by coefficient according to which
component of the mixture that coefficient currently occupies, and the conditioning on
$\gamma$ makes that precision a fixed, known matrix at the moment this draw is taken.
:::

### Result R-11.3: the indicator's conditional as prior odds times a Bayes factor

Conditional on $\beta_j$, the indicator $\gamma_j$ depends on the data only through
$\beta_j$, since $\gamma_j$ merely labels which mixture component generated it. Its
full conditional is Bernoulli with odds
$$
\frac{\Pr(\gamma_j = 1 \mid \beta_j)}{\Pr(\gamma_j = 0 \mid \beta_j)}
= \frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\cdot\frac{1}{c}\cdot
\exp\left\{\frac{\beta_j^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\tau_j^2}-\frac{1}{c^2\tau_j^2}\right)\right\}.
$$
Integrating $\beta_j$ out of this conditional, rather than fixing it at its current
draw, turns the same odds into a genuine Bayes factor between two marginal models,
$$
\mathrm{BF}_j = \sqrt{\frac{1+v_0 S_j/\sigma^2}{1+v_1 S_j/\sigma^2}}\;
\exp\!\left\{\frac{(x_j^\top r_j)^2}{2\sigma^2}\left[\frac{v_1}{\sigma^2+v_1 S_j}
-\frac{v_0}{\sigma^2+v_0 S_j}\right]\right\}, \qquad
\frac{\Pr(\gamma_j=1\mid r_j,\sigma^2)}{\Pr(\gamma_j=0\mid r_j,\sigma^2)}
= \frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\,\mathrm{BF}_j,
$$
with $v_0=\tau_j^2$, $v_1=c^2\tau_j^2$, $S_j = x_j^\top x_j$, and $r_j$ the partial
residual after every other coefficient's current fit is subtracted off. The square-root
factor is an Occam penalty that shrinks towards zero as the slab widens, so an
uninformative slab is not a neutral choice but an active vote against inclusion.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The conditional form follows Bayes' rule applied to the two densities
$p(\beta_j \mid \gamma_j = 1) = \phi(\beta_j; 0, c^2\tau_j^2)$ and
$p(\beta_j \mid \gamma_j=0) = \phi(\beta_j; 0, \tau_j^2)$: the posterior odds of the
indicator are the prior odds $\pi/(1-\pi)$ times the ratio of these two densities at the
current $\beta_j$, and writing out the Normal densities the normalising constants leave
a factor $\sqrt{\tau_j^2/(c^2\tau_j^2)} = 1/c$ while the exponents combine into the
displayed quadratic form in $\beta_j^2$.

For the integrated version, fix every coefficient except the $j$-th and define the
partial residual $r_j = y - \sum_{k\neq j}x_k\beta_k$, so $r_j = x_j\beta_j+\varepsilon$.
Conditional on $\gamma_j = g$ and $\sigma^2$, both the likelihood of $r_j$ given
$\beta_j$ and the prior for $\beta_j$ are Normal, and their convolution is Normal too,
$r_j \mid \gamma_j=g,\sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^2 I_n + v_g x_j x_j^\top)$. The
matrix determinant lemma gives $\det(\sigma^2 I + v_g x_jx_j^\top) = (\sigma^2)^n(1+v_g
S_j/\sigma^2)$ and the Sherman-Morrison formula inverts the covariance in closed form;
substituting both into the multivariate Normal density and keeping only the terms that
depend on $g$ gives
$$
\log p(r_j\mid\gamma_j=g,\sigma^2) = -\tfrac12\log\!\left(1+\frac{v_gS_j}{\sigma^2}\right)
+\frac{v_g(x_j^\top r_j)^2}{2\sigma^2(\sigma^2+v_gS_j)} + \text{terms free of }g.
$$
The Bayes factor is the difference of this at $g=1$ and $g=0$, exponentiated, which is
the displayed $\mathrm{BF}_j$. The square-root factor is smaller than one whenever
$v_1>v_0$: a wide slab spreads its prior mass over coefficient values the data did not
produce and pays for that in the marginal likelihood, exactly the Occam-razor
mechanism behind the g-prior penalty of the exercise session's continuous-shrinkage
material. Pushing $v_1\to\infty$ with everything else fixed sends the square root to
zero while the exponential term converges to a finite limit, so the Bayes factor
vanishes for every data set: an uninformative slab is Lindley's paradox in its
variable-selection form, an aggressive vote against inclusion rather than a neutral
one, which is why $c$ must be set to an economically meaningful effect size rather than
made as large as possible.
:::

Together, R-11.2 and R-11.3 give a complete Gibbs sweep: draw $\beta$ given $\gamma$ and
$\sigma^2$ from the Normal of R-11.2, draw $\sigma^2$ given $\beta$ from its ordinary
inverse-Gamma full conditional exactly as in Lecture 2, and draw $\gamma$ given $\beta$
from the Bernoulli of R-11.3, one coordinate at a time since the $p$ indicators are
conditionally independent given $\beta$. Averaging the indicator draws over a long chain
gives, for each candidate, its posterior inclusion probability, the object Section 6
reports for every one of the forty-eight industries.

## Data: forty-eight industry portfolios and one banking target {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the Kenneth French forty-nine industry portfolios,
`data/ff_industry49_monthly.parquet`, together with the risk-free rate from
`data/ff_factors_monthly.parquet` used to convert returns to excess returns. The banking
portfolio is the target throughout; the other forty-eight portfolios are the candidate
regressors, and no other variable is used anywhere in this chapter.

```{python}
#| label: fig-target-series
#| fig-cap: "Monthly excess return on the banking industry portfolio, training and held-out periods shaded separately."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(y_raw.loc[:SPLIT].index, y_raw.loc[:SPLIT].to_numpy(), color="steelblue", lw=0.6,
        label="training (to 2009-12)")
ax.plot(y_raw.loc["2010-01":].index, y_raw.loc["2010-01":].to_numpy(), color="firebrick",
        lw=0.6, label="held out (2010-01 onward)")
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.6)
ax.set_ylabel("banking excess return"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("Banking industry portfolio, monthly excess return")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

y_te_raw, X_te_raw = y_raw.loc["2010-01":].to_numpy(), X_raw.loc["2010-01":].to_numpy()
Xi_te, yi_te = (X_te_raw - mx) / sx, (y_te_raw - my) / sy
print(f"training sample: {n_i} months, {exc.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {SPLIT}, "
      f"mean {y_tr_raw.mean():.4f}, sd {sy:.4f}")
print(f"held-out sample: {len(yi_te)} months, 2010-01 to {exc.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"candidate correlations with the target: "
      f"min {min(np.corrcoef(Xi[:, j], yi)[0,1] for j in range(p_i)):.3f}, "
      f"max {max(np.corrcoef(Xi[:, j], yi)[0,1] for j in range(p_i)):.3f}")
```

The estimation sample runs $480$ months from January 1970 to December 2009, split
deliberately before the global financial crisis so that the entire post-crisis period,
including its aftermath, is held out for scoring rather than fitting. Both sides of the
split are standardised using training-sample moments only, so no information from the
held-out block leaks backward into the estimation. The banking portfolio earned $0.0048$
a month in excess of the risk-free rate over the training period with a standard
deviation of $0.0624$, and every one of the forty-eight candidates is positively
correlated with it, from $0.148$ to $0.809$, which is what a shared equity market factor
produces and is exactly why a plain correlation ranking, of the kind a naive screen
would run, cannot by itself separate a genuine channel from a proxy for the market as a
whole.

## Empirical analysis: running stochastic search on forty-eight industries {#sec-empirical}

### The sampler

The spike standard deviation is $\tau=0.02$ and the slab factor is $c=20$, so a
coefficient is called excluded when it sits within about two hundredths of a target
standard deviation of zero, and a prior inclusion probability of $\pi=0.2$ means about
ten of the forty-eight industries are expected to matter a priori.

```{python}
def ssvs_sampler(X, y, pi_prior=0.2, tau_s=0.02, c_s=20.0, alpha_0=3.0, delta_0=0.1,
                 n_iter=8000, burn=2000, rng=None):
    n_s, p_s = X.shape
    XtX_s, Xty_s = X.T @ X, X.T @ y
    log_prior_odds = np.log(pi_prior) - np.log1p(-pi_prior) - np.log(c_s)
    slab_gain = 0.5 * (1.0 / tau_s ** 2 - 1.0 / (c_s * tau_s) ** 2)
    beta_s, gamma_s, sig2 = np.zeros(p_s), np.ones(p_s, dtype=bool), float(np.var(y))
    bd = np.empty((n_iter, p_s)); gd = np.empty((n_iter, p_s), dtype=bool)
    sd = np.empty(n_iter)
    for t in range(n_iter):
        d_s = np.where(gamma_s, (c_s * tau_s) ** 2, tau_s ** 2)
        L = np.linalg.cholesky(XtX_s / sig2 + np.diag(1.0 / d_s))
        b1 = np.linalg.solve(L.T, np.linalg.solve(L, Xty_s / sig2))
        beta_s = b1 + np.linalg.solve(L.T, rng.standard_normal(p_s))
        r_s = y - X @ beta_s
        sig2 = 1.0 / rng.gamma(alpha_0 + n_s / 2, 1.0 / (delta_0 + 0.5 * r_s @ r_s))
        gamma_s = rng.random(p_s) < 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(
            -(log_prior_odds + slab_gain * beta_s ** 2)))
        bd[t], gd[t], sd[t] = beta_s, gamma_s, sig2
    return bd[burn:], gd[burn:], sd[burn:]

b_ind, g_ind, s2_ind = ssvs_sampler(Xi, yi, rng=rng)
pip_i, mean_i, size_i = g_ind.mean(axis=0), b_ind.mean(axis=0), g_ind.sum(axis=1)
print(f"kept {len(size_i)} draws; posterior sigma^2 {s2_ind.mean():.4f} "
      f"(residual sd {np.sqrt(s2_ind.mean()):.4f} target sd)")
print(f"model size: mean {size_i.mean():.2f}, median {np.median(size_i):.0f}, "
      f"90% interval [{np.quantile(size_i,0.05):.0f}, {np.quantile(size_i,0.95):.0f}]")
print(f"distinct visited models: {len(np.unique(g_ind, axis=0))}")
```

The posterior residual variance is a fraction of the target's own variance, so the
included industries between them explain most of the banking portfolio's monthly
movement; the model-size interval says the posterior is not confident about how many
industries belong, and the count of distinct visited models says the sampler is
genuinely wandering the space rather than sitting on one model with occasional
excursions.

### Posterior inclusion probabilities and the median probability model

```{python}
ordi = np.argsort(-pip_i)
tbl = pd.DataFrame({"industry": [ind_names[j] for j in ordi[:10]],
                    "PIP": pip_i[ordi[:10]].round(3),
                    "post mean": mean_i[ordi[:10]].round(3),
                    "corr with target": [round(float(np.corrcoef(Xi[:, j], yi)[0, 1]), 2)
                                        for j in ordi[:10]]})
print(tbl.to_string(index=False))
mpm_i = pip_i >= 0.5
print(f"\nmedian probability model ({mpm_i.sum()} industries): "
      f"{[ind_names[j] for j in np.where(mpm_i)[0]]}")
print(f"remaining {p_i - mpm_i.sum()} candidates: max PIP {pip_i[~mpm_i].max():.3f}, "
      f"mean PIP {pip_i[~mpm_i].mean():.3f}")
```

The median probability model keeps six industries. Trading and financial services and
insurance are included in essentially every draw; paper and steel follow at high but not
unanimous inclusion probabilities; laboratory equipment and textiles sit just above the
one-half threshold. The other forty-two candidates have a maximum inclusion probability
well below one half and an average close to zero, so the data have argued most of the
industry universe out of the regression. Steel is the sharpest illustration that this
is not a correlation ranking in disguise: its raw correlation with banking returns is
the lowest of the six selected, and its posterior mean coefficient is negative, entering
not because it moves with banks but because, once the financial industries have
absorbed the common exposure, steel's remaining variation is a useful control for the
cyclical component the financials over-represent.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pip-and-size
#| fig-cap: "Left: posterior inclusion probability for all 48 candidate industries. Right: posterior distribution of the number of included industries."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4))
cols = ["firebrick" if v >= 0.5 else "0.6" for v in pip_i]
axes[0].bar(np.arange(p_i), pip_i, color=cols)
axes[0].axhline(0.5, color="black", ls="--", lw=1, label="median-probability threshold")
axes[0].axhline(0.2, color="C2", ls=":", lw=1.2, label="prior inclusion probability")
axes[0].set_xticks(np.arange(p_i)); axes[0].set_xticklabels(ind_names, rotation=90, fontsize=5)
axes[0].set(ylabel="posterior inclusion probability", title="PIPs for 48 candidate industries")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].hist(size_i, bins=np.arange(size_i.min(), size_i.max() + 2) - 0.5,
             density=True, color="steelblue", alpha=0.85)
axes[1].axvline(size_i.mean(), color="black", ls="--", lw=1, label=f"mean {size_i.mean():.1f}")
axes[1].set(xlabel="number of included industries", ylabel="posterior probability",
            title="Posterior distribution of model size")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The left panel shows the shape a real selection problem has: a handful of bars well
above the threshold, a long grey floor at or below the prior probability, and two or
three bars in the awkward middle that are neither clearly in nor clearly out. The right
panel shows model size spread over a wide range rather than concentrated at one value,
which is another way of saying the posterior is choosing a distribution over lists, not
a single list.

### Correlated candidates: substitution, not absence

A low marginal inclusion probability can mean a candidate is irrelevant, or it can mean
the candidate is a close substitute for something else already in the model. The two
look identical in a table of marginal PIPs and different in the joint distribution of
the indicators.

```{python}
def pair_table(gd, pip, pairs):
    rows = []
    for a, b in pairs:
        ja, jb = ind_names.index(a), ind_names.index(b)
        rows.append({"pair": f"{a} / {b}", "corr": round(float(C_ind[ja, jb]), 2),
                     "PIP A": round(float(pip[ja]), 3), "PIP B": round(float(pip[jb]), 3),
                     "both": round(float((gd[:, ja] & gd[:, jb]).mean()), 3),
                     "if independent": round(float(pip[ja] * pip[jb]), 3),
                     "either": round(float((gd[:, ja] | gd[:, jb]).mean()), 3)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

pairs_i = [("steel", "labeq"), ("bussv", "labeq"), ("fin", "insur")]
print(pair_table(g_ind, pip_i, pairs_i).to_string(index=False))
```

Steel and laboratory equipment, correlated candidates both associated with the
industrial cycle, appear together noticeably less often than independence would
predict, while financials and insurance, also correlated, appear together in every
draw because the posterior wants both of them unconditionally rather than competing for
a single slot. Correlation alone does not produce substitution; substitution happens
when two correlated candidates are competing for a marginal place in the model.

```{python}
b_tight, g_tight, _ = ssvs_sampler(Xi, yi, pi_prior=0.01, rng=rng)
pip_tight = g_tight.mean(axis=0)
print(f"prior inclusion probability 0.01: mean model size falls to "
      f"{g_tight.sum(axis=1).mean():.2f}")
print(pair_table(g_tight, pip_tight, [("steel", "labeq")]).to_string(index=False))
```

Tightening the prior inclusion probability shrinks the mean model size and sharpens the
competition: places in the model become scarce, and the steel and laboratory-equipment
pair now appears together far less often than independence would predict even though
each individually still has a non-trivial inclusion probability. Reporting the two
marginal probabilities separately, without the joint table, would suggest that one of
the pair is a clear inclusion and the other a clear exclusion, when the honest summary
is that the posterior wants one member of the pair in the model and is close to
agnostic about which.

### Out of sample against unrestricted least squares

```{python}
def oos_r2(b):
    e = yi_te - Xi_te @ b
    return 1.0 - e @ e / (yi_te @ yi_te)

b_mpm_i = np.zeros(p_i)
b_mpm_i[mpm_i] = np.linalg.solve(XtX_i[np.ix_(mpm_i, mpm_i)], Xty_i[mpm_i])
print(pd.Series({"SSVS (model averaged)": oos_r2(mean_i),
                 "SSVS median-probability model": oos_r2(b_mpm_i),
                 "OLS (all 48)": oos_r2(b_ols_i)},
                name="held-out predictive R^2").round(4).to_string())
print(f"absolute weight on the {p_i - mpm_i.sum()} excluded industries: "
      f"SSVS {np.abs(mean_i[~mpm_i]).sum():.3f}, OLS {np.abs(b_ols_i[~mpm_i]).sum():.3f}")
```

Model-averaged SSVS beats both the median-probability model and unrestricted least
squares out of sample, and the gap traces directly to the last line: least squares
carries a substantial total absolute weight on industries the posterior says contribute
essentially nothing, and that weight is exactly the extra variance that hurts a forecast
without buying any bias reduction in return.

```{python}
#| label: fig-oos-cumulative
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative squared forecast error, 2010-01 onward, for the model-averaged SSVS posterior and unrestricted least squares."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for b, lbl, col in [(mean_i, "SSVS (model averaged)", "steelblue"),
                    (b_ols_i, "OLS (all 48)", "0.55")]:
    e = (yi_te - Xi_te @ b) ** 2
    ax.plot(np.arange(1, len(e) + 1), np.cumsum(e), label=lbl, color=col, lw=1.4)
ax.set(xlabel="held-out month", ylabel="cumulative squared forecast error",
       title="Out-of-sample error, 2010-01 onward")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The two curves separate steadily across the held-out period rather than in one episode,
so the advantage is not an artefact of a single unusual month.

## Discussion: what the sampler found, and what it cannot rule out {#sec-discussion}

Six industries survive stochastic search out of forty-eight: the two financial
industries closest to banking in business model, a couple of industrial and materials
industries that plausibly proxy for the aggregate cycle, and two entries closer to the
awkward middle of the posterior than to confident inclusion. That is a defensible,
economically legible answer to the question this chapter opened with, and it forecasts
better out of sample than keeping everything, which is the check against something
already known: a model that both makes economic sense and predicts well is stronger
evidence than either property alone.

The limitation is what the posterior inclusion probabilities do and do not certify.
They say which candidates this particular design, this particular prior and this
particular sample support; they do not say the excluded industries have no economic
relationship to banking, only that the relationship is not separable, in this design,
from the six that were kept, and the correlated-pair analysis showed exactly why:
substitution can drive a genuinely relevant channel's marginal probability down without
the channel being absent. Nor does a short, confident list mean the underlying world is
sparse; a design that gave sparse selection every advantage would still return a short
list even in a world where every coefficient is a little bit non-zero, because the
spike-and-slab prior is built to produce short lists and a moderate predictive margin
over an unrestricted fit is not strong enough evidence to tell the two worlds apart.

There is a limitation of a different kind that this chapter has not touched at all.
Every posterior in this chapter, and in every chapter before it, has been built on a
single error variance $\sigma^2$ held fixed across the whole sample. Equity returns are
not like that: the banking portfolio's volatility in 2008 bears no resemblance to its
volatility in 1995, and a model that cannot let the error variance move is misspecified
in a way no amount of variable selection can repair, because the wrong assumption lives
in the likelihood, not in which regressors are included. Lecture 12 takes up exactly
that problem.

1. By hand. Using the orthogonal-design argument sketched in the moved
   continuous-shrinkage material, show that under $X^\top X = nI_p$ the model-averaged
   predictor and the median-probability model coincide with the Bayes-optimal single
   model exactly when every posterior inclusion probability is zero or one, and say
   what breaks in that argument once two columns are correlated.

2. Computational. The simulated factor-committee exercise moved to the session builds a
   design with known true coefficients, known decoys, and known noise, and asks you to
   recover the truth with SSVS and to compare it against the continuous shrinkage
   alternative and the g-prior marginal likelihood derived in R-11.3's callout.
   Reproduce it and report how the sparse-versus-dense predictive margin changes as the
   number of truly active coefficients grows.

3. On real data. The macroeconomic companion moved to the session asks which lags of
   industrial production growth, inflation, unemployment, the term spread and the
   funds rate belong in a forecasting equation for industrial production growth.
   Reproduce it and report which lagged variables the sampler selects, and whether any
   pair of adjacent lags shows the same complementary pattern, jointly included far more
   often than their marginals alone would suggest, that the industry data showed for
   correlated substitutes.
